notes.b: Expenditure is the money a household spends, and income sets the limit on it. Spending that goes beyond income leads to debt, so spending must be matched to income, and many factors shape how a household divides its money.
points: Low-income households spend most of their income on essentials such as housing, food and heat, and a larger proportion on food than richer households do, so they have little or no discretionary spending (spending on non-essentials) or saving.

Higher-income households spend more in total and a bigger share on discretionary items such as leisure, holidays and eating out, so they have more discretionary income (money left after essentials) and can also save and pay for credit.
Family size and composition matter, for example the number of children and whether it is a one-parent or two-parent household, because each extra person adds to food, clothing and housing needs.
The stage of the family life cycle changes priorities: young children add costs for food, clothing, childcare and schooling, while teenagers cost more for food, clothing and education.
Once children are independent and at retirement, spending falls and shifts towards health, leisure and heating; older children can also help decide and manage spending.

Employment affects money, travel time and cost, and meal and sleep patterns. Working outside the home adds travel, convenience food and childcare costs, and shift work changes meal and sleep patterns and transport costs.

Urban and rural location change patterns, for example through transport costs and housing costs: rural households depend more on cars, while urban rents and mortgages are higher. Heating costs also differ.

Other influences include socio-economic class and the gender of the earner, personal values and priorities, health or special needs, advertising and peer pressure (the influence of friends and others the same age).
notes.tip: If asked how income, family stage and personal values affect spending, say that income sets the total, the life-cycle stage changes the needs, and values shape priorities. At Higher Level, give a reason and a consequence for each influence, not just its name.

notes.b: Not all spending is equally urgent. Households divide it into what they must pay to manage family life and what they can choose to spend once the necessities are covered.
points: Essential expenditure is spending on necessities needed to manage family life, such as housing (rent or mortgage), utilities (electricity, heating), food, clothing, transport, insurance, medical bills, loan repayments and household bills.
Discretionary expenditure is spending on non-essentials, made only after essential expenditure and savings have been provided for.
Examples of discretionary expenditure: holidays, entertainment, alcohol, cosmetics, eating out, leisure and gym membership, and streaming services.
Fixed essential costs stay the same amount at regular times each week or month, such as rent or a mortgage repayment, insurance and telephone bills, so they are easy to plan for.

Irregular essential costs vary in amount or timing, such as clothing, doctor's bills, school expenses and car repairs, so a budget must set money aside for them. Some are also seasonal, such as heating, Christmas and back to school.

Whether an item is essential depends on the household. The same item can be essential for one household and discretionary for another, for example a car for a rural family compared with a city family.
Credit repayments are fixed commitments in the budget, and credit used for essentials adds to future spending because it must be paid back.
notes.tip: Differentiate essential and discretionary spending with an example of each, then add the fixed and irregular split of essential costs to earn full marks. Never classify a car as always essential or always a luxury, because it depends on the household.

notes.h: Planning a personal or family budget
notes.b: A budget is a plan that sets expected net income against planned spending for a period such as a week, month or year. Following a series of steps means essentials are paid first and money is left for savings.
points: 1. List all income, using net (take-home) income, never gross, because net income is the money actually available to spend. Include wages, welfare, maintenance and any other income.
2. List planned fixed, irregular and discretionary expenditure for each week or month, including credit repayments, and choose the time period the budget will cover.
3. Plan essential needs first, such as rent or mortgage and household bills, before any discretionary spending, so the necessities are always covered.
4. Allocate money for short-term and long-term savings, and for emergencies, so unexpected costs do not have to be borrowed.
5. Allow for personal spending and special occasions such as Christmas and holidays, and for changes in circumstances, so these annual costs do not cause a shortfall.
6. Keep bills and receipts, and record one month of actual spending to find where overspending occurs.

7. Compare income with expenditure and adjust. A surplus (income greater than spending) can be saved; a deficit (spending greater than income) means cutting discretionary spending, raising income or seeking advice, rather than borrowing.
8. Review the budget regularly, and change it when family circumstances or income change, so it stays realistic.
notes.tip: A budget is a plan, and a record of actual spending is a check on it, so you need both. If asked for three steps, give estimating net income, listing all expenditure, and allocating and reviewing. At Higher Level, include fixed, irregular and discretionary spending, Christmas, savings, personal spending and review.

notes.b: When a budget shows overspending or a deficit, a household can cut costs without going without essentials. The savings come from shopping smarter and using less.
points: Use a shopping list and stick to it, because this avoids impulse buying of items you did not plan to purchase.
Choose own-brand goods and compare prices between shops, since similar goods can cost much less.
Buy second-hand or in charity shops, use sales, and buy food in season, when it is cheaper and plentiful.
Cook from scratch and choose cheaper cuts of meat, because convenience foods and prime cuts cost more.
Cut energy use and switch supplier to reduce utility bills.
Cancel unused subscriptions, such as gym membership or streaming services, so you are not paying for things you do not use.
notes.tip: When asked to describe ways a consumer could reduce expenditure, give a developed point for each: shopping list, own brand, second-hand, bulk buying, cheaper cuts and energy saving.

notes.b: A budget does more than record numbers. It shows a household where its money goes and helps it avoid problems before they happen.
points: Budgeting shows where money goes, and identifies overspending and impulse buying before they lead to unplanned debt.
Budgeting reduces reliance on credit and supports a good credit record, because bills and repayments are planned for and paid on time.
A budget gives financial security and reduces the worry and stress caused by unpaid bills, because it ensures bills are paid.
A budget that allows some saving can provide for emergencies and cover unexpected events, such as job loss or an urgent repair.
Budgeting helps a household reach its goals, because money is set aside for them.
Budgeting builds money-management skills that transfer to independent living.
notes.tip: If asked to discuss four advantages of budgeting, give a developed sentence for each, not a list: reduces overspending, avoids debt and impulse buying, provides for emergencies, reduces stress and builds money skills.

notes.b: A sample budget shows how a net income can be divided between headings so that every euro is planned. The first sample is a family of two adults and two children with a combined net income of 900 euro a week.
points: Housing, the largest fixed essential cost, is allocated about a quarter of income (25 per cent): 225 euro.
Food is allocated about a quarter of income (25 per cent): 225 euro, because food needs rise with growing children.
Household bills are allocated about 15 per cent of income: 135 euro. Education is allocated about 10 per cent: 90 euro, to cover school costs.
Clothing, leisure, savings, health and discretionary spending are each allocated about 5 per cent: 45 euro each, with savings kept for emergencies.
A second sample, 800 euro a week for the same type of family, gives 200 euro for housing, 200 for food, 120 for household bills, 80 for education and 40 for each of the five 5 per cent headings.
The totals must add up to the net income, so the plan allocates the full net income, leaves no money unplanned, and is reviewed each month.
The percentages are a planning guide for this sample, not a rule, and should be adjusted to the family's actual fixed costs.
A lower income cannot cover the same percentages, so essentials come first while discretionary spending and savings shrink; a higher income allows more savings.
notes.tip: In a weekly budget for a stated family and income, make the allocations add up to the net income, show a percentage and a euro amount under each heading, and include savings and discretionary lines. At Higher Level, give a reason for each allocation and a note on review. Never present 25/25/15/10/5 as a rule for every family.

notes.b: Households that are in debt, or at risk of it, can get free help from MABS. It advises and negotiates for them but does not lend money or pay their debts.
points: MABS is a free, confidential and independent service for people in debt or at risk of debt, funded by the State through the Citizens Information Board.
MABS helps a household work out its income and spending, and draws up a realistic budget and repayment plan (schedule) with the family.
MABS negotiates with lenders, including moneylenders and mortgage lenders, on behalf of households in debt.

MABS offers a mortgage arrears service, and advises on personal insolvency (when a person cannot pay their debts) and income maximisation, which means checking and claiming entitlements to State supports.
MABS advises on financial products and interest rates, and points to cheaper sources of credit such as credit unions.
MABS also teaches money-management skills, so households can manage their budgets themselves in future.
notes.tip: When describing the role of MABS, mention that it is free, independent and confidential, then budgets and repayment schedules, debt advice, negotiating with lenders, mortgage arrears, income maximisation, and credit unions and interest rates. Do not say MABS lends money or pays debts for the client.

keyTerms.definition: Spending on necessities such as housing, utilities, food, clothing, transport and medical bills.
Spending on non-essentials, made only after essential expenditure and savings have been provided for.
Essential costs that stay the same each week or month, such as rent or a mortgage repayment.
Essential costs that vary in amount or timing, such as clothing or school expenses.
A plan that matches planned income to planned spending over a set period.
The stage a household has reached, such as young children, older children or retirement, which changes its spending priorities.
Savings set aside to cover unexpected costs such as job loss or an urgent repair.
The Money Advice and Budgeting Service, a free and independent Irish service that helps households with debt and budgeting.

factCards.term: Five factors that affect spending patterns
factCards.definition: Socio-economic class, urban or rural location, gender of the earner, family size and life-cycle stage.

factCards.term: Three examples of fixed essential costs
factCards.definition: Rent or mortgage repayments, insurance premiums and telephone bills.

factCards.term: Three examples of irregular essential costs
factCards.definition: Clothing, doctor's bills and school expenses.

factCards.term: Four guidelines for drawing up a budget
factCards.definition: Plan essential needs first; allow for short-term and long-term savings; keep receipts and records; review the budget regularly and change it when circumstances change.
Debt advice; budgeting and repayment schedules; negotiation with lenders; income maximisation.
Financial security; avoids overspending and impulse buying; reduces reliance on credit; reduces stress.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by fixed essential expenditure and irregular essential expenditure, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Fixed essential expenditure: necessary costs that stay the same each week or month, for example rent or a mortgage repayment, an insurance premium or a telephone bill. Irregular essential expenditure: necessary costs that vary in amount or timing, for example clothing, a doctor's bill or school expenses. One example given for each type.

questions.prompt: A family of two adults and two children has a fixed net income each month. Describe the steps the family should take to draw up a budget that avoids debt, and explain how the budget should be reviewed. Refer to the role of MABS for a family that is already in debt.
questions.model: Steps: list all net income; list planned fixed, irregular and discretionary expenditure; plan essentials first (housing, food, household bills); allocate savings for the short and long term and for emergencies; allow for personal spending and special occasions; keep bills and receipts and record a month of spending to find overspending. Review: check the budget regularly against actual spending and change it when income or family circumstances change. Reasons: budgeting reduces reliance on credit and reduces stress. MABS: a free, independent service that helps with debt, budgeting and repayment schedules, negotiates with lenders, supports mortgage-debt resolution and personal insolvency, and maximises income.
